multiplechoiceresponse.p: A language model writes a fluent paragraph citing a policy that does not exist. This is best described as:

choice.div: Confabulation — plausible text that is not grounded in fact.
A deliberate lie by the model.
A sign the model has no training data.

div.p: The model optimises for plausible continuation, not truth. Every citation, number and policy claim must be checked against a source.

multiplechoiceresponse.p: Why is a polished, confident answer not evidence that it is correct?

choice.div: Fluency is cheap for these systems; correctness requires grounding.
Because confident answers are usually wrong.
Because the model refuses to answer uncertain questions.

div.p: Polish is the model's default output. It does not carry a reliability signal, so the reader must supply the check.

multiplechoiceresponse.p: You ask the same question in two new chats and get different details. What does that tell you about relying on the answer?

choice.div: The output is sampled, so anything you rely on must be pinned and verified.
One of the answers must be from a different model.
The second answer is the corrected one.

div.p: Non-determinism is normal. If an output matters, save it, check it, and treat the saved version as the artifact.

choiceresponse.p: Which are sound uses of a language model at work? Select all that apply.

choice.div: Drafting a first version of an email you will edit and check.
Reformatting notes you supply into an outline.
Generating practice questions a person will review.
Answering a customer's policy question without checking the policy.

div.p: Drafting, reformatting and option generation work on material you bring and leave judgement with you. Policy answers must come from the policy.
